title: Allah, the One
hook: one, eternal, merciful, like nothing else

segments.voice: Yesterday, iman, and your line: six to believe. Could you still count them at a red light? Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, the decree. Today, the first. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

How short can a description of God be? The Qur'an has a chapter that gives one in four short verses. It's called al-Ikhlas, sincerity, and it sits near the very end of the book, small enough to learn in a sitting and said in prayer. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions it is equal to a third of the Qur'an. Four verses, worth a third. Today, the first article of faith, through that tiny chapter.
screen: `HOW SHORT CAN IT BE?` → `FOUR VERSES.` → `EQUAL TO A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in Pickthall's translation. "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." Take it a line at a time. First, one. Not one among several, and not the first of a series. Muslims call this tawhid, oneness, and it's the center of everything else on the list of six. Second, eternally besought. The Arabic word is as-Samad, and translators struggle with it. Pickthall's eternally Besought of all points to the one everyone turns to, who needs nothing from anyone. Every other thing leans on something. This one doesn't lean. Third, nothing like Him. Another verse says it plainly: "Naught is as His likeness." Some readers see here one reason Islamic art leaves out pictures of God and turns to calligraphy and pattern instead. Fourth, merciful. The surah doesn't say it, but the line said before surah after surah does: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Oneness in Islam isn't cold. The One is also the one who is gentle. And a word about the name. Allah is the Arabic word for God. Arabic-speaking Christians say Allah too, in their prayers and their Bibles, and Arabic-speaking Jews have used it as well. The name is shared; what Muslims say about Him is in those four verses.
screen: `ONE, NOT ONE OF MANY.` · `THE ONE ALL TURN TO.` · `NAUGHT IS AS HIS LIKENESS.` · then, large: `THE ONE IS MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with oneness. Notice how many things are in your mind right now: a message to answer, a sound outside, a worry. Don't fight them. Just let them be many. Then pick one thing to rest on: your breath, or the single word one. Each time the many pull you away, come back to the one. If you pray, you can recite al-Ikhlas slowly, or simply the word Allah. If you don't, the word one is enough. The bell holds the time.
Allah. The Arabic word for God; in the Qur'an, the One, the eternally besought, with none comparable unto Him. Today's word.
Your line: one. Today, when your attention splits into ten pieces, say the word one and pick the next single thing. Tomorrow, the second article: the angels. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah al-Ikhlas often, in daily prayers and at other times, and the oneness of God, tawhid, stands at the center of Islamic belief.

fork.setup: a friend asks how the Qur'an sums up God in a few lines. what do you point to?
options: a long list of names and deeds.
four verses: one, besought of all, not begetting nor begotten, none comparable.
a picture of a king on a throne.
fork.reveal: Surah al-Ikhlas does it in four short verses, and a hadith says they equal a third of the Qur'an.

original.note: Arabic: God; the word Arabic-speaking Muslims, Christians and Jews use for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: Allah is the name of a god only Muslims worship.
what it means: Allah is the Arabic word for God, the One of Surah al-Ikhlas, used by Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians too.
what a scholar hears: tawhid, and the hard word as-Samad, which translators render in several ways.
